transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess I’m here because... honestly, I’ve been trying for months now to get people to just sit down and understand what is actually happening, and I'm at my wit's end. It’s my husband’s family. They have been quietly—and I mean very, very carefully and deliberately—messing with our money and ruining our good name. And nobody wants to see it! 

I work as a billing clerk, you see, so I look at numbers and ledgers all day long, I know how these systems operate. And lately, I’ve started noticing these little billing errors showing up at work. Tiny things, the kind of things a normal person might just brush off as a computer glitch or a typo, but I know better. I know they are doing it to make me look incompetent, to mess with my job and our finances. 

And it’s spilling over into everything else, too, which is just so unfair. Like at church, people who I’ve known for years are suddenly acting completely funny toward me. Just last week, people were practically turning their backs when I walked up, giving me these strange looks, and I know it’s because his family has been getting to them, whispering things to ruin my reputation in the community. I’ve tried to explain this, I’ve tried to show my husband and my boss the connections, but no matter what records anyone pulls up—they’ll show me a bank statement or a work log and say, 'Look, it’s just a clerical mistake'—but I know it isn't. I know exactly how it all ties back to his family, and it's like I'm the only one who can see the pattern.
Have you heard voices when no one else was there?

Voices? No... no, nothing like that. I mean, I know exactly why you’re asking me that, I really do. Because when you try to tell people that you’re being targeted, or that someone is messing with your life, they immediately want to put you in a little box and say, 'Oh, she must be hearing things, she’s losing her grip.' But my mind is perfectly sound, Doctor. I don't hear voices in my head or anything out of a movie. 

When I'm sitting alone in my living room, it is completely quiet. Well, except for the traffic, since we live right off the main road, and maybe the refrigerator humming—we have this older model that makes a terrible racket when the ice maker kicks on—but that's it. I don't hear things that aren't there. 

The problem isn't imaginary voices, it's the real voices. It's the actual whispers I hear when I walk past the breakroom at work, or the hushed conversations my husband's family has when they think I'm out of earshot in the kitchen. I have very good hearing, actually. I had it tested a couple of years back when I had a bad sinus thing, and the doctor then said my hearing was exceptional for my age. So when I hear people talking about me, or when I hear that specific tone in my boss's voice when he brings up one of those supposed 'clerical errors' on the ledgers, I know exactly what I'm hearing. It's all very real. I really don't need to make up voices when the real people around me are already doing enough damage, you know?
Has anything happened that you believe would be impossible by ordinary means, like someone controlling your thoughts or sending you special messages?

Oh, heavens no. Impossible by ordinary means? No, no, no. I mean, I watch a lot of television, I see those sci-fi shows my husband likes to put on—the ones with the mind control and the telepathy and the aliens sending signals through the TV set—and I can assure you, nothing like that is happening to me. My life is very ordinary, almost boringly ordinary, except for this whole nightmare with his family. 

Nobody is controlling my thoughts. My thoughts are my own, thank you very much. And as for special messages... well, I mean, I don't get secret codes through the radio or anything ridiculous like that. The messages I get are very plain and very ordinary. Like when my sister-in-law leaves a passive-aggressive comment on my Facebook page, or when my boss sends an email about "attention to detail" and CCs the whole department. Those are messages, sure, but they aren't supernatural. They are just cruel. They are just ordinary people doing ordinary, nasty things to try and push me out. 

I really think people want to believe that I'm talking about magic or mind control because it's easier to write me off that way. If I say, "My husband's family is manipulating my finances and ruining my reputation," people don't want to deal with the messy reality of that. It's so much easier for them to just say, "Oh, she thinks she's getting messages from space." But I don't. I just look at the bank statements, and I look at the ledgers at work, and I look at the way people treat me at church, and I see the very real, very human, very ordinary sabotage that is happening right in front of me. There's nothing impossible about it at all. It's just devastatingly effective.
Even when other people show you records that seem to disprove it, do you still feel completely certain that your husband’s family is behind this?

Well, yes, absolutely. I mean, I know what they’re showing me. I’m not blind. When my boss, Mr. Henderson—who I’ve worked for, by the way, for going on nine years now, and he knows my work is impeccable—when he calls me into his office and pulls up the screen and points to a misplaced decimal point on the Peterson account, I see the decimal point. I see that it looks like a typo. And when my husband pulls up our joint checking account on his phone and says, 'Look, honey, the balance is fine, the mortgage cleared on the 14th just like always,' I see the numbers. 

But you have to understand, Doctor, seeing the numbers and understanding what’s actually happening behind the numbers are two completely different things. It’s like... well, it’s like looking at a beautiful painting and thinking it’s just a picture of a house, but not realizing the artist painted it to cover up a crack in the wall. They show me these records—the bank statements, the work logs, the church directory, whatever it is—and they think that’s the end of the story. They think because a piece of paper says one thing, that it proves I’m wrong. 

But I know how these systems work. I’m a billing clerk! I spend eight hours a day, sometimes nine if it’s the end of the month and we’re closing out the books, looking at how data moves from one column to another. I know how easy it is for someone who is determined, someone who is quietly and carefully trying to ruin you, to manipulate those things. So when they show me a record that supposedly disproves what his family is doing, all it really proves to me is how deep his family has gotten into everything. It just shows me how good they are at covering their tracks. 

Because I know what I know. I know why that woman from the choir committee wouldn't look me in the eye on Sunday, and I know why those 'little errors' keep showing up under my login at work. It all ties back to them. And honestly, it’s exhausting trying to explain this to people who just want to look at a piece of paper and say everything is fine, when I can see the whole pattern right there in front of me. So yes, I am completely certain. The records don't change the truth.
How long have you been certain that your husband’s family is behind this?

Well, it really started... let me think. It's been about nine months now. Yes, nine months, because it all really kicked off around the holidays last year. You see, there was this whole big blow-up with his family over money, and who was hosting what, and the expectations they put on us. His mother, especially, has these grand ideas about how things should be done, and she expects everyone to just fall in line and foot the bill, regardless of what our actual budget looks like. 

And I remember, it was right around Thanksgiving, because I had spent three days—three whole days—prepping my house for them to come over. I cleaned the baseboards, I ironed the good napkins, the ones we got for our wedding that we never use, and I bought this expensive organic turkey because his sister is suddenly very particular about what she eats. And then, at the dinner table, the comments started. Just these little, biting remarks about our house, and my job, and how we manage our finances. 

That was the turning point. That was when I realized they weren't just difficult in-laws. That was when I saw the actual malice. And ever since then—for these last nine months—it’s been a constant, steady campaign against me. First, it was the cold shoulders at family gatherings, then it was the strange issues with our bank accounts that my husband always tries to brush off, and then, of course, the trouble started at work. It all stems from that holiday disaster. They realized I wasn't going to just roll over and let them dictate our lives and our finances, so they decided they had to get rid of me. Nine long, exhausting months of this, Doctor. And nobody seems to understand how draining it is to have to be on guard every single day since then.
Aside from this problem with your husband’s family, has your ability to manage your job and daily responsibilities changed much?

Well, no, not really. I mean, if you looked at my day-to-day schedule, you wouldn't think anything was wrong at all. I still get up every single morning at 6:15 AM sharp, just like I have for the last fifteen years. I make my coffee, I get dressed, and I go to work. And at the office, I am still handling all my billing clerk duties just fine, thank you. I'm processing the invoices, I'm matching up the purchase orders, I'm reconciling the daily batches at the end of the shift. I haven't missed a beat there, despite those little "typos" I mentioned earlier. I just double-check everything now. 

And it’s the same thing at home. I keep the house going exactly as I always have. The laundry is done on Saturdays, the floors are vacuumed twice a week, and I still make sure there’s a hot dinner on the table, even if my husband is acting distant. I even make sure to carve out time for myself, because you have to, don't you? A person needs an outlet with this kind of stress. So I still spend a lot of time out in the garden. Right now, I'm working very hard on my hydrangeas, trying to get the soil pH just right so they bloom that really deep, beautiful blue. It takes a lot of aluminum sulfate and patience, let me tell you. And if the weather is bad, I stay inside and do my watercolor painting. It's very soothing. 

So my ability to manage my life? It’s perfectly intact. The only time... well, the only time I actually run into any trouble during my day is when I try to explain things to people. When I try to warn them about what my in-laws are doing. 

That’s when the problems start. If I try to pull my supervisor aside and explain exactly *why* those errors are showing up under my login, or if I try to tell my sister or the ladies at church about the financial manipulation so they can be on their guard, that’s when things get tense. People just... they get so uncomfortable. They don't want to hear it, or they interrupt me, or they look at me with this awful pity, like I'm the one causing a scene. That is the only real disruption to my daily life, Doctor. Just the absolute brick wall I hit when I try to warn people about the truth. But as far as my actual responsibilities go? No, I handle all of that just fine.
During these past nine months, have you had a period of at least several days when you felt unusually energetic and needed much less sleep than usual?

Well, no. No, I haven't had anything like that. I mean, unusually energetic? Needing less sleep? Heavens, no. If anything, I'm just so tired. Like I was saying, it is absolutely exhausting having to be on guard all the time. I still get my solid seven or eight hours of sleep a night, usually. Well, I try to. Sometimes I lie awake for a bit, just turning things over in my mind, you know, thinking about what his mother said or what that look from my boss really meant. But I certainly don't feel energetic. 

And I've never been one of those people who can just run on three hours of sleep and a cup of coffee. My sister is like that—she's a nurse, works the night shift sometimes, and I swear she just buzzes around the next day like it's nothing. But not me. I need my rest. Especially now, with everything that's going on, I need my wits about me. If I don't get a good night's sleep, how am I supposed to catch the little things they're doing? How am I supposed to spot the discrepancies in the billing logs if my eyes are tired? 

So no, definitely no periods of feeling super energetic or not needing sleep. It's just been a steady, draining slog for these past nine months, just trying to keep my head above water and keep everything running smoothly at home and at work while they do their level best to undermine me. I just feel... normal, energy-wise, I suppose. Just a normal person dealing with an abnormal amount of stress.
Before these last nine months, have you generally tended to distrust other people and suspect they had bad motives?

No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, before all of this started nine months ago, I was probably too trusting. I really was. I've always been the kind of person who takes people at their word. You know, if someone says they're going to do something, I believe them. If someone smiles at me, I assume they're being friendly. I mean, I've lived in the same neighborhood for twelve years, and I've always been on good terms with the neighbors. We wave when we get the mail, we chat over the fence about the weather or the garden—like Mrs. Gable next door, she’s always asking about my hydrangeas, and I never once thought she had some ulterior motive for asking. I just thought she liked flowers. 

And at work, before the holidays last year, I never suspected anyone of anything. I just went in, did my billing, and assumed everyone else was doing their jobs just as honestly as I was. I mean, you have to have a certain level of trust to function in society, don't you? You have to believe that the bank teller isn't stealing your deposit, or that the mechanic isn't cutting your brake lines. And I did! I really did. 

Even with my husband's family... I mean, we always had our little disagreements, sure. What family doesn't? His mother has always been a bit overbearing, and his sister can be very self-centered, but I just chalked it up to personality differences. I thought, "Well, that's just how they are," and I tried to be the bigger person. I never, ever thought they were actively plotting against me. I never thought they were capable of this kind of... of coordinated malice. 

So, no, I haven't always been distrustful. It's only been since I saw the truth of what they were doing. It's like a veil was lifted, Doctor. Once you see that kind of betrayal from your own family—well, your in-laws, anyway—it changes you. It forces you to look at everything differently. Because if the people who are supposed to be family can do this to you, can manipulate your finances and try to ruin your career, then who *can* you trust? But before that? No, I was perfectly trusting. Too trusting, obviously, or I might have seen this coming sooner.
Has anyone told you that your speech or your thinking has become hard to follow or disorganized?

Well, no. No, nobody has ever said anything like that to me. I mean, disorganized? Hard to follow? If anything, I think my thinking is the most organized it has ever been in my entire life. You have to be, don't you? When you're dealing with the kind of situation I'm dealing with, you simply cannot afford to have disorganized thoughts. I keep everything very, very straight in my head. 

And at work, like I said, I'm a billing clerk. Communication is key in that department. When I'm typing up an email to a vendor about a mismatched purchase order or explaining a batch error to the front office, I have to be crystal clear. I use bullet points, I reference the exact invoice numbers, I highlight the discrepancies... my supervisor has always praised my attention to detail. So my speech and my writing are perfectly fine. 

Now, like I mentioned just a few minutes ago, sometimes people *act* like they don't understand me, but that's not because I'm not making sense. That’s just them choosing not to listen. When I try to sit my husband down and explain the timeline to him—you know, I'll say, "Look, your mother came over on Tuesday, she was asking all those pointed questions about our savings, and then suddenly on Wednesday my work login is acting up"—I lay it out so logically. Step one, step two, step three. Anyone with half a brain could follow it. I even draw the connections for them so there's absolutely no confusion. 

But he just... he gets this blank look on his face, or he sighs heavily and tells me to drop it. My sister does the same thing, she just changes the subject. But that is not me being hard to follow, Doctor. That is willful ignorance on their part. They just don't want to engage with the facts because the facts are uncomfortable. But as far as my actual ability to put a sentence together or organize my thoughts? No, absolutely not. I am perfectly, one-hundred-percent clear.
Has your husband’s family ever done anything to you that you believe would be impossible for ordinary people to do?

Impossible? Like... like science fiction or magic? Heavens, no. No, I'm not saying they have superpowers or anything ridiculous like that. They're just ordinary people. But they are ordinary people who are incredibly, incredibly spiteful and organized. I mean, that is exactly why I’m here, Doctor. Because for months now—months and months—I’ve been trying to get people, anyone, to just sit down and understand that my husband’s family is quietly messing with our money and our good name. It doesn't take magic to do that. It just takes malice. 

Like, I'll be at work—and you know I'm a billing clerk, I've been doing this for years, I know my job inside and out—and suddenly these little billing errors will just... show up. A transposed number here, a deleted line item there in the posting log. Just enough to make me look careless, to jeopardize my job and our livelihood. And then outside of work, it's my reputation. We'll be at Sunday service, and suddenly someone at church, someone I’ve known for years, just acts completely funny toward me. Won't meet my eye during the fellowship hour, or gives me this tight little polite smile and quickly walks away. 

And people will say to me, 'Oh, it's just a computer glitch,' or 'Oh, she was just having a bad morning, don't take it personally.' But it's not a coincidence! It is all connected. And the most exhausting part is that they are so, so careful about covering their tracks. No matter what records anyone pulls up—whether it's the IT logs at work showing a supposed system error, or my husband checking his mother's phone bill to prove she hasn't been calling my coworkers or the ladies at church—they make sure their fingerprints aren't on it. They probably use prepaid phones or have someone else do the actual tampering. But I know it ties back to them. I know it does. You don
Have you ever believed your husband’s family was doing something to you that would be impossible in ordinary life?

I... wait, didn't we just cover this? I feel like you just asked me that, Doctor. Like I was just saying, no. Absolutely nothing impossible. I mean, what do you even mean by impossible? If you mean are they using magic wands or, I don't know, beaming things through the television set, then of course not. I'm a perfectly rational person. 

Everything they are doing is completely, one-hundred-percent grounded in reality, which is exactly why it is so incredibly frustrating that my husband won't just open his eyes and look at the evidence! If I were sitting here telling you that his mother was walking through walls or flying on a broomstick, I could understand people looking at me funny. I really could. But what they are doing is completely possible for anyone with a little bit of time and a whole lot of spite. 

Just think about it for a second. How hard is it, really, to mess with someone's life in this day and age? My mother-in-law has been in my house hundreds of times over the years. She could have easily peeked over my shoulder when I was checking my work email or paying the utility bills at the kitchen island. That island, by the way, is right next to the living room sofa where she always insists on sitting—specifically so she can critique my housekeeping, I’m sure, but it also gives her a perfect view of my laptop screen. It doesn't take a superhero to memorize a password. It just takes a sneaky person. 

And as for the rumors and the way people are treating me at church, well, gossip is the oldest trick in the book, isn't it? You don't need to defy the laws of physics to whisper a few choice lies to the ladies on the altar guild or pull the pastor aside after Sunday service and plant a seed of doubt about my character. People do that every day. It's just... it's all so painfully ordinary, really. Just ordinary, cruel people doing ordinary, cruel things to ruin my life, and using completely normal methods to do it. So no, nothing impossible at all. Just highly, highly orchestrated.
Did this belief about your husband’s family start suddenly over a day or two, or did it build up gradually?

Well, it certainly did not just pop into my head overnight, if that is what you are asking. It was not like I just woke up one Tuesday and suddenly thought they were out to get me. No, it has been going on for about nine months now. I can trace it back exactly to the source, Doctor, because it all started right after we had this massive falling out over money and her ridiculous holiday expectations. 

You see, about nine months ago, my mother-in-law decided she wanted us to host the entire extended family for the holidays. And I am not just talking about a nice little dinner for five or six people. I mean everyone. Cousins, aunts, people my husband barely even speaks to during the rest of the year. She wanted it fully catered, she wanted new floral arrangements, and she fully expected us to foot the entire bill. Now, I handle the finances in our house. Like I said, I work in billing, I know how to manage a ledger and keep things balanced. So I sat down, I ran the numbers, and I told my husband that we simply could not afford to drain our savings just to put on a show for his mother. I put my foot down. I told her no, we are not spending our money that way and she would have to adjust her expectations.

Well, let me tell you, she did not like that one bit. She gave me this tight little smile and said she understood, but I saw the look in her eyes. It was pure ice. And ever since that exact conversation, for nine solid months, my life has been an absolute nightmare. That is when the little errors at work started showing up on my computer. That is when the ladies at church started turning their backs on me during fellowship hour. It was a direct retaliation. So it built up gradually in terms of what they were doing to me, yes, but the campaign itself started exactly nine months ago because I dared to set a boundary about our money. And she has been making me pay for it every single day since.
Over these months, have you noticed yourself becoming much less emotionally expressive or less interested in being around other people than you used to be?

Less emotionally expressive? Goodness, no. I... I don't even know why you would ask that. If anything, Doctor, I am feeling *more* emotions these days. I mean, how could anyone possibly be flat or unemotional when their entire life, their livelihood, their good name in the community is under constant, organized attack? I am stressed, I am frustrated, I am angry—and I am certainly expressing it! Just ask my husband. I am constantly trying to get him to see how upsetting this all is. I'll be practically in tears at the kitchen island, pointing out the suspicious things happening or the way his mother looked at me, and I am very, very expressive about how much it hurts. 

And as for not wanting to be around people? No, that is not it at all. I have always been a social person. I loved my church group, I loved the fellowship hour, I used to really enjoy organizing the potlucks and chatting with everyone. I *want* to be around people. I really do. It's just... well, it's not that I've lost interest in *them*, it's that she has poisoned them against *me*. I still force myself to go to service every single Sunday because I refuse to let her win and run me out of my own congregation. I still walk right up to the ladies at the altar guild and try to strike up a normal conversation about the weather or the scripture reading. 

But it is incredibly draining to try and be social when you know—you just *know*—that they've been fed a bunch of lies about you. It takes so much energy to put on a brave face when someone gives you that tight little polite smile and scurries away because of whatever my mother-in-law whispered to them. So if I seem a little guarded sometimes, it's not because I don't care about being around people anymore. It's just self-preservation, really. I would love nothing more than to just have my normal social life back, exactly the way it was before she started this whole nightmare.
During these nine months, have you been depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Depressed? No... no, I wouldn't use that word at all. I mean, sure, there are days when I just want to pull my hair out, but that's not depression, Doctor. That's just a completely normal reaction to being targeted. If I were depressed, I'd probably just be lying in bed all day, wouldn't I? Staring at the ceiling, crying over absolutely nothing. But I'm not crying over nothing. I'm dealing with a very real, very active campaign to ruin my life. 

I still get up every single morning at 6:00 AM sharp. I make my coffee—just half a cup, because too much caffeine makes me jittery when I have to focus on the billing ledgers at work—and I go to my job, and I do my absolute best despite the little traps she's setting for me. So, no, not depressed. Angry? Yes. Exhausted? Absolutely. I mean, who wouldn't be exhausted when you have to double-check every single invoice you post because you know someone is trying to make you look incompetent? 

But I don't sit around feeling sorry for myself or feeling sad for no reason. I simply don't have the time to be depressed! I have to stay vigilant. Because if I let my guard down and just sink into some kind of funk, she wins. And I am absolutely not going to let a woman who threw a temper tantrum over holiday catering run me into the ground. So, no, I haven't been depressed. Just highly, highly stressed out by what she is doing to my life.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a fixed, highly systematized persecutory belief that her husband’s family is sabotaging her finances, job performance, and reputation despite repeated contradictory evidence. The belief has persisted for about 9 months, is non-bizarre/plausible in content, and occurs without hallucinations, thought disorder, negative symptoms, mania, or major depressive episode. Functioning is largely preserved outside the direct impact of the delusional belief, supporting persistent delusional disorder.
